The same pair of hyperplanes must work for all the measures, and no perpendicularity condition is imposed. What is the exact value of \(D_s\) as a function of \(s\)?

15	## 1. Upper bound: \(D_s\le 3n-2\)
16	
17	Set \(d=3n-2\), and let \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_j\) be the given measures.
18	
19	Parametrize oriented affine hyperplanes, including two constant limiting forms, by
20	\[
21	u=(a,b)\in S^d\subset\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R,
22	\qquad h_u(x)=a\cdot x+b.
23	\]
24	Write \(\sigma_u(x)=\operatorname{sign}h_u(x)\). Define
25	\[
26	F(u,v)=
27	\left(
28	 \int\sigma_u\,d\mu_i,\ 
29	 \int\sigma_v\,d\mu_i,\ 
30	 \int\sigma_u\sigma_v\,d\mu_i
31	\right)_{i=1}^j.
32	\]
33	This is continuous: a nonconstant affine form vanishes on a Lebesgue-null hyperplane, whereas a constant form arising here is \(1\) or \(-1\); dominated convergence therefore applies everywhere.
34	
35	Changing \(u\) to \(-u\) reverses the first and third entries of each triple. Changing \(v\) to \(-v\) reverses the second and third. Consequently, on
36	\[
37	X=\mathbb RP^d\times\mathbb RP^d,
38	\]
39	the map defines a section of the real vector bundle
40	\[
41	E=\left(L_1\oplus L_2\oplus(L_1\otimes L_2)\right)^{\oplus j},
42	\]
43	where \(L_1,L_2\) are the two tautological line bundles.
44	
45	Here are the standard characteristic-class facts needed:
46	\[
47	H^*(X;\mathbb F_2)
48	 =\mathbb F_2[x,y]/(x^{d+1},y^{d+1}),\qquad
49	w_1(L_1)=x,\quad w_1(L_2)=y.
50	\]
51	First Stiefel–Whitney classes add under tensor products of line bundles, and total classes multiply under direct sums. Thus
52	\[
53	w_{3j}(E)=x^jy^j(x+y)^j.
54	\]
55	A nowhere-zero section would split off a trivial line from \(E\), forcing this top class to vanish.
56	
57	It does not vanish. The coefficient of \(x^d y^{d-2}\) is
58	\[
59	\binom{j}{n}=\binom{2n-2}{n},
60	\]
61	which is odd. Indeed, since \(n\) is a power of two, over \(\mathbb F_2\)
62	\[
63	(1+t)^{2n-2}=1+t^2+t^4+\cdots+t^{2n-2}.
64	\]
65	Both exponents \(d,d-2\) survive the cohomology-ring truncation.
66	
67	Therefore \(F\) has a zero. At this zero neither affine form is constant, and Fourier inversion on the four sign choices gives
68	\[
69	\mu_i\{\sigma_u=\varepsilon,\sigma_v=\delta\}
70	=\frac14\left(
71	1+\varepsilon\int\sigma_u\,d\mu_i
72	+\delta\int\sigma_v\,d\mu_i
73	+\varepsilon\delta\int\sigma_u\sigma_v\,d\mu_i
74	\right)
75	=\frac14.
76	\]
77	All four sign regions are nonempty and convex. They are exactly the four connected components of the hyperplane complement. This proves the upper bound.

79	## 2. A nonsingular bilinear construction
80	
81	For the lower bound, write
82	\[
83	k=\frac n2-1\ge1,
84	\]
85	so \(n=2k+2\) and \(j=4k+2\).
86	
87	Let \(V\) be the real vector space of complex polynomials of degree at most \(k\). Its real dimension is \(n\). For
88	\[
89	p(z)=\sum_{r=0}^k p_rz^r
90	\]
91	use the norm
92	\[
93	N(p)=\sum_{r=0}^k|p_r|^2.
94	\]
95	Put \(U(z)=1+z^{2k}\), and define a symmetric real-bilinear map into the complex polynomials of degree at most \(2k\):
96	\[
97	B(p,q)=pq-\operatorname{Re}\langle p,q\rangle\,U,
98	\qquad
99	\langle p,q\rangle=\sum_{r=0}^k p_r\overline{q_r}.
100	\]
101	Its target has real dimension \(4k+2=j\).
102	
103	### Claim
104	\[
105	B(p,q)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p=0\ \text{or}\ q=0.
106	\]
107	
108	Let \(t=\operatorname{Re}\langle p,q\rangle\). If \(t=0\), then \(pq=0\), proving the claim.
109	
110	Otherwise,
111	\[
112	pq=t(1+z^{2k}).
113	\]
114	Both factors have degree exactly \(k\), and all their roots lie on the unit circle. Hence the reversed-conjugate polynomial
115	\[
116	q^*(z)=z^k\overline{q(1/\bar z)}
117	\]
118	has the same roots as \(q\), so \(q^*=cq\) for some nonzero constant \(c\). But
119	\[
120	\langle p,q\rangle=[z^k](pq^*)
121	=c[z^k](pq)=0,
122	\]
123	because \(k\ge1\) and \(1+z^{2k}\) has zero coefficient at \(z^k\). This contradicts \(t\ne0\), proving the claim.
124	
125	## 3. Turning the construction into positive-definite forms
126	
127	Let \(F_1,\ldots,F_j\) be all the real and imaginary coefficient functions of
128	\[
129	F(p)=p^2-N(p)U.
130	\]
131	Their polarizations are the coordinates of \(B\), so they have no common bilinear zero with both arguments nonzero.
132	
133	Define
134	\[
135	H(p)=-\operatorname{Re}[z^0]F(p)
136	     -\operatorname{Re}[z^{2k}]F(p)
137	=2N(p)-\operatorname{Re}(p_0^2+p_k^2).
138	\]
139	Thus \(H(p)\ge N(p)\).
140	
141	Every coefficient of \(p^2\) has absolute value at most \(N(p)\), by Cauchy–Schwarz. Consequently,
142	\[
143	F_i(p)\ge-2N(p).
144	\]
145	The quadratic forms
146	\[
147	C_i(p)=3H(p)+F_i(p),\qquad 1\le i\le j,
148	\]
149	are therefore positive definite:
150	\[
151	C_i(p)\ge N(p)>0\qquad(p\ne0).
152	\]
153	
154	They still have no common nonzero bilinear zero. Indeed, if all their polarizations vanish at \((p,q)\), write \(h=H(p,q)\). Then
155	\[
156	F_i(p,q)=-3h\quad\text{for every }i.
157	\]
158	Since \(H\) is minus the two real endpoint coordinates,
159	\[
160	h=-(-3h)-(-3h)=6h.
161	\]
162	Thus \(h=0\), all \(F_i(p,q)=0\), and the preceding claim applies.
163	
164	Identifying \(V\) with \(\mathbb R^n\), we have constructed positive-definite symmetric matrices \(C_1,\ldots,C_j\) such that
165	\[
166	a^{\mathsf T}C_i b=0\quad\text{for every }i
167	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=0\ \text{or}\ b=0. \tag{*}
168	\]
169	
170	## 4. Gaussian counterexamples in dimension \(3n-3\)
171	
172	Work in
173	\[
174	\mathbb R^{3n-3}=\mathbb R^{j-1}\oplus\mathbb R^n.
175	\]
176	Take \(j\) Gaussian probability measures with means
177	\[
178	(0,0),(e_1,0),\ldots,(e_{j-1},0),
179	\]
180	and respective covariance matrices
181	\[
182	I_{j-1}\oplus C_1,\ldots,I_{j-1}\oplus C_j.
183	\]
184	All these measures have smooth, everywhere-positive densities.
185	
186	Suppose two affine hyperplanes equipartitioned them. Each hyperplane would bisect every Gaussian. A hyperplane bisects a nondegenerate Gaussian exactly when it passes through its mean. Passing through all the displayed means forces both hyperplanes to have equations
187	\[
188	a\cdot z=0,\qquad b\cdot z=0,
189	\]
190	where \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(a,b\ne0\).
191	
192	For the \(i\)-th Gaussian, the two linear forms are centered jointly Gaussian, with covariance \(a^{\mathsf T}C_i b\). A centered bivariate Gaussian has four equal sign probabilities exactly when its correlation is zero; explicitly,
193	\[
194	\Pr(X>0,Y>0)=\frac14+\frac{\arcsin\rho}{2\pi}.
195	\]
196	Thus equipartition would imply
197	\[
198	a^{\mathsf T}C_i b=0\qquad(1\le i\le j),
199	\]
200	contradicting \((*)\).
201	
202	So the required property fails in dimension \(3n-3\). The property is monotone in dimension: project measures onto a smaller-dimensional coordinate space, partition there, and lift the hyperplanes. Hence failure in dimension \(3n-3\) excludes every smaller dimension as well.
203	
204	Combining the two bounds gives
205	\[
206	\boxed{D_s=3n-2=3\cdot2^{s-1}-2}.
207	\]
